topic: What if you could shrink anything?
title: WHAT IF YOU COULD
SHRINK ANYTHING?

script.text: Too much to pack? Shrink. It all fits.

script.beat: 1 cold open, demo 2 (useful, and the first hint of the cost)
script.text: Couch stuck on the stairs? Shrink. Still heavy.
Annoying little sister? Shrink. Uh oh.
What if you could shrink anything?

script.beat: 4 the turn: the cost, one real fact
script.text: One catch: things get smaller, never lighter. Shrink the Earth to sixteen millimetres, a marble, and it's a black hole. That's real.
So why is the floor cracking?

science.claim: Shrink the Earth to sixteen millimetres (a marble) and it's a black hole.
science.working: A mass becomes a black hole once it fits inside its Schwarzschild radius, r = 2GM/c^2. For Earth: 2 x 6.674e-11 m^3 kg^-1 s^-2 x 5.972e24 kg / (2.998e8 m/s)^2 = 7.971e14 / 8.988e16 = 8.87e-3 m, so a radius of 8.87 mm, a diameter of 17.7 mm. A standard marble is 16 mm (5/8 inch) across, a radius of 8 mm, which is inside 8.87 mm: all of Earth's mass in a 16 mm ball is a black hole. The schematic shows 16 mm and the 17.7 mm limit.
science.source: Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c^2; Earth's mass 5.972e24 kg (NASA Earth Fact Sheet); G and c from CODATA 2018; standard marble size 5/8 inch (16 mm)

science.working: The power's rule, and the honest version of shrinking: scaling a thing down doesn't remove any of its matter, so its mass (and its weight) stays the same while its volume falls with the cube of the scale. At x0.05 a thing's volume is 0.05^3 = 1/8000 of what it was, so it is 8,000 times denser.
science.source: Conservation of mass; density = mass / volume, volume scales with length cubed

shots.note: Juno leans on an overflowing suitcase on the bed; the lid springs back up
the caliper clamps the heap of clothes; it squeezes down into the case
the case shut with room to spare; Juno zips it round, smug; a pink tag: CLOTHES x0.28
a couch wedged across the stairs; Juno shoves from below, it won't move
the caliper clamps the couch; it squeezes to a toy and drops onto the tread
Juno lifts the toy couch one-handed; his arm drops like it's full size; tag: STILL 40 kg
Bea dances on the island; Juno in the foreground has had enough; the cat watches
the caliper clamps Bea mid-dance; she squeezes to mouse size
tiny Bea looks up; the cat's huge head slides into frame
the premise over the city at night; Juno with the toy couch and tiny suitcase
a balance: the big couch and the toy couch weigh the same, 40 kg each
the Earth in the calipers squeezes to 16 mm; the loupe shows it beside a marble
the sheet floods with ink; the Earth caves in to a black hole; r < 8.87 mm
Juno, worried; his paper edge turns pink
the toy couch on the floor; the boards crack out from under it; Juno backs off
